verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains that the Romans, whose empire extended to the Levant, had been defeated by the Persians in territory apparently referring to the Hejaz, but were promised victory within bidʿ, or three to nine years. The first and third pronouns in “they will be victors” refer to the Romans. Although some take the intervening pronoun in ghalabihim to refer to the Persians, it may also refer to the Romans if ghalab signifies the object (mafʿūl); thus, the preferred meaning is that the Romans would be victorious after their own defeat.

“All command belongs to Allah, before and after” means that command belongs to God both before the Roman defeat and afterwards: He does what He wills, granting victory or casting down whom He wills. This reading is preferable to one that makes “before” the time of their defeat and “after” the time of their victory. “On that day” is connected with the faithful rejoicing, as is God’s help: when the Romans prevail, the faithful will rejoice at God’s help of them.

verses.5:
Al-Mizan takes “He helps whomever He wishes” as a new sentence confirming that all command belongs to God. As the All-mighty, He makes mighty whom He wills by His help (naṣr); as the All-merciful, He singles out whom He wills for mercy.

It rejects readings that attach “on that day” to “before and after,” since this separates the latter part of the verse from the former; or that connect “at Allah’s help” to the faithful rather than to their rejoicing, since this would make their rejoicing at the Roman victory arbitrary, given that every victory is from God. It also rejects identifying this help with the faithful’s victory at Badr, for that does not accord with “He helps whomever He wishes,” and does not consider worthy of attention readings that make it the fulfilment of the Roman prophecy or God’s granting ascendancy to some disbelievers over others.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan explains “Allah’s promise” as an emphatic absolute object: God has made a promise, specifically the preceding promise that the Romans will be victorious and the faithful will rejoice. “Allah does not break His promise” further confirms it.

Although breaking a promise may sometimes be right in an emergency, God faces no emergencies; moreover, breaking a promise implies deficiency, and God has none. Since He declares that He does not break His promises and is the most truthful of speakers, it is impossible for Him to break one. Most people do not know this because they are ignorant of God’s nature and judge Him by themselves, imagining that He may sometimes speak truly or falsely and keep or break promises.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse is more apparently an exceptional clause explaining why people do not know that God’s promise is true, that all command is His before and after, and that He will help the faithful against the faithless. Zamaksharī, in al-Kashshāf, instead treats “They know” as a permutation of “do not know,” showing that ignorance and knowledge confined to this world are alike.

The indefinite “an outward aspect” stresses the meagerness of their knowledge. Its outward aspect (ẓāhir), opposed to its inward aspect (bāṭin), consists of worldly vanities perceived by the senses. Pursuing them throughout life, people forget the life beyond this world and its knowledge, and so fail to know what truly benefits them. The proposed meaning of ẓuhūr as zawāl, making their knowledge merely fleeting, rests on a very uncommon usage of ẓāhir.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan explains that the heavens, earth, and all between them—the visible world—were created bi al-ḥaqq, not idly, but for a real purpose realized through their existence. Because neither the world nor its parts are eternal, and no transient part can be the ultimate end of another, their intended goal becomes manifest only after the world passes away. “For a specified term” therefore indicates that the world will end, while the purpose for which it was created endures: this purpose is the Hereafter.

“Have they not reflected in their own souls?” is an expression of amazement and means reflecting with a clear, focused mind. Occupation with worldly life scatters the mind and makes people, as it were, absent from themselves; attentive reflection leads them to truth. Another interpretation takes the phrase to mean reflection on the originated (muḥdath) soul, which would infer an eternal, living, powerful, knowing, wise, and needless Originator (muḥdith), then religion, testing, righteous works, reward (thawāb), and the Hereafter. Al-Mizan rejects this reading because it leaves no relation between the opening phrase and the statement that the heavens and earth were created in truth and for a specified term.

The “encounter” (liqāʾ) with the Lord is return to Him at the Resurrection. The verse ends, as it began, in amazement: having begun with Him, how can people disbelieve in returning to Him?
verses.9: Al-Mizan says that, after mentioning widespread denial of the Resurrection, the verse recalls earlier nations and the terrible punishments that overtook them so that people may take warning and abandon disbelief. Those nations were stronger and developed the land more extensively: “ploughing the earth” means turning it over for agriculture, construction, and the like. Though their messengers brought manifest proofs, their punishment was not wrongdoing by God; they wronged themselves through disbelief and sin.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains that “then” introduces the outcome of the wrongdoers. Misfortune (sawʾā) is a harmful deficiency and here means divine punishment; the phrase about denying God’s signs gives its cause. Thus their exclusive fate was the worst punishment because they denied and derided God’s signs.

A possible alternative makes their fate the denial and derision themselves, so that their misdeeds led them into still worse disbelief. Although plausible, Al-Mizan prefers the first reading because the context warns and teaches a lesson by declaring that the outcome of misdeeds is divine punishment.
verses.11: Al-Mizan concludes that the beginning and end of all creatures are in God’s hand: He originates them, restores them, and brings them back to Himself. Here khalq means creatures (makhlūqūn), which accounts for the plural pronoun in the conclusion.
verses.12: Al-Mizan explains that when the Hour comes—the time when guilty sinners return to God for reckoning and recompense—they will despair of His mercy. The word yublis encompasses every kind of misery.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains that the guilty will lose hope not only of God’s mercy for their own deeds but also of the intercession they expected from the gods they associated with God and worshipped as intercessors. Through worshipping these partners, they were disbelievers and veiled from God.
verses.14: Al-Mizan explains that, when the Hour comes, the faithful who performed righteous deeds will be separated from guilty sinners: the former enter heaven and the latter hell. Majmaʿ al-Bayān defines rawḍa as a garden of the greatest beauty and pleasantness, while al-Rāghib in the Mufradāt explains yuḥbarūn as rejoicing until the embellishments of their comfort appear to them. The necessary division of the faithful and the evildoers is itself a proof of the Resurrection: they cannot rightly be treated as equal in life and death.

verses.17:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as the conclusion to the account of creation, return to God, and the separation of the faithful from the faithless. Paradise belongs to those who have faith and do righteous deeds, while those who denied God’s signs and the Hereafter, despite worldly power and wealth, receive the worst punishment—utter annihilation in this world—for wronging themselves, not because God wronged them. Creation follows a supremely exalted divine plan, whereas human beings have associated partners with God, denied their encounter with Him, and committed other misdeeds.

The verses therefore instruct the audience to glorify God as they are renewed moment by moment and to praise His governance of the entire visible world. He is free of their false beliefs and immoral acts, and praiseworthy for all that He creates and directs. They are God’s own instruction to say “glory to God” and “to God belongs all praise,” not a quotation of someone else, and concern glorification and praise generally, not specifically the daily obligatory prayers.

“To Him belongs all praise in the heavens and the earth” is an interjection. Thus “at nightfall and when you enter noontime” continues “when you enter evening and when you rise at dawn”: all times are for glorification and all places for praise. The creation and command throughout heaven and earth belong solely to God, and their beauty calls for praise and magnification. The view that all things praise and glorify God merely by existing, through their poverty and deficiency before His perfection, is not what these verses express.

The adverbial use of ʿashiyyan reflects that its root cannot be conjugated on the pattern of ifʿāl, unlike the terms for evening, morning, and noontime. The plural address broadens an address initially directed to the Prophet to human beings generally; it is not a transition (iltifāt) between addressees.

verses.19:
Al-Mizan takes the apparent meaning of bringing forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living to be the creation of life from non-living earth and the transformation of living creatures into non-living earth. It has also been interpreted as the believer emerging from the disbeliever and the disbeliever from the believer, with “living” and “dead” used figuratively.

Reviving the earth means producing green vegetation in spring and summer after its barrenness in autumn and winter. Likewise, people will be brought from their graves and raised to a new life, just as the earth is revived after death.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan explains that humanity’s creation from dust means that the human form is constituted from earthly elements throughout its worldly stages and finally returns to them. The particle behold (idhā) expresses surprise: inanimate matter would be expected to remain inanimate, yet it becomes living, sentient, thinking human beings who scatter over the earth, ultimately destroying life. Thus the phrase has the sense of: Then We produced him as another creature! (23:14).

The gathering of earthly components and their transformation into a living, feeling, thinking human being is a sign of a wise, living Creator who directs the universe’s natural order. Then (thumma) marks both an interval and the sequence of events; the clause beginning with it is connected to He created you from dust, rather than to Of His signs is that He created you.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan, citing al-Rāghib, notes that zawj denotes either the male or female partner among sexual animals. God created mates for human beings from their own species and for their benefit. Man and woman can produce offspring only together; each is incomplete and in need of the other, while their union forms a complete unit capable of producing a child. Their movement toward one another and the peace they find together arise from the implanted instinct by which what is incomplete seeks wholeness and what is needy seeks fulfilment.

The commentary takes affection (mawadda) to be love’s visible practical expression, just as humility (khuḍūʿ) manifests the inward awe (khushūʿ) produced before greatness. Mercy (raḥma) is the psychological response to seeing another’s deficiency and need, which moves one to remove that deprivation and fulfil the need. The family is its clearest instance: spouses are joined by love and affection, and both—especially the wife—mercifully protect, nurture, shelter, and educate children unable to meet their own needs. Without such mercy, the human race would cease. Affection and mercy also operate socially, in care for the poor, infirm, and weak.

From the verse’s context, the intended affection and mercy apparently concern the family; read independently, the verse also implies the wider social meaning. Reflection on the two sexes, households, the affection and mercy that foster societies, the continuation of the species, and the fulfilment of people in this world and the next reveals astonishing signs.
verses.22: Al-Mizan apparently understands the difference of tongues as the diversity of languages and colors as the distinction of racial groups. As scholars have also said, tongues may include differences of accent, tone, and manner of speech, while colors may refer to each individual’s distinct shade of skin. Those who study the macrocosm find in its natural order subtle signs whose artifice and power can come from, and return to, none but God.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan explains that grace (faḍl), literally what exceeds need and hence a possible gift, here means sustenance (rizq); pursuing God’s grace is seeking one’s livelihood. Human nature contains a force that drives people to strive for their daily needs, then to cease striving, rest, remove fatigue, and renew their strength. The succession of night and day, assigned respectively to rest and effort and made possible on earth through the movement of heavenly bodies, is a sign for one who listens attentively, reflects on what is heard, and follows it when it is found true.

Al-Zamakhsharī reports in al-Kashshāf that the wording envelops the times of night and day with the activities occurring in them: sleep and seeking grace are mentioned, while the two complementary activities are separated by the two times, because time and its contents are effectively inseparable. The verse could instead mean sleep in both times and pursuit of sustenance in both, but he holds the first meaning more apparent, since it recurs often in the Qur’an and is especially pertinent. This explains the ending directed to a people who listen.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan holds without doubt that He shows you at the opening of the verse functions in place of an infinitive, as do the openings of the preceding verses. It is also possible that an implicit “that” (an) follows the verb, yielding the sense that He shows you the lightning; the accusative form in some recitations strengthens this possibility. Other proposed constructions—an implicit possessive construct, making of His signs the object of the verb, or treating it as adverbial for lightning—are highly unlikely, and some disrupt the verse’s coherence with those before it.

Fear and hope mean fear of thunderclaps and hope for rain. God sends down water and revives the dead earth with it; those who apply reason recognize in these phenomena a divine intelligence, rather than benefits arising by coincidence.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan explains that “standing” (qiyām), opposed to sitting (quʿūd), is the most upright human posture and is therefore used metaphorically for being firmly established and for administering another’s affairs. The standing of heaven and earth by God’s command means that all their motion and rest, change and stability are firmly established by that command, whose nature is that when God wills something, He says to it “Be,” and it is.

In then (idhā), when He calls you, calling forth from the earth, behold (idhā), you will come forth, the first idhā is conditional, while the second expresses surprise and functions as the particle introducing the consequence. From the earth qualifies calling forth. Although this sentence is grammatically joined to the preceding one, it is not joined to it in meaning: it concerns Resurrection and return to God, not one of the signs. The interpretation that makes coming forth from the earth another sign alongside the standing of heaven and earth is rejected, because Resurrection is among the three fundamental beliefs, with Divine Unity and Prophethood, to which the signs point. It cannot itself be a sign for Divine Unity; rather, Divine Unity points to Resurrection.

The preceding signs all concern the ordering of human affairs: humanity’s earthly origin, the two sexes, linguistic and color differences, sleep, seeking sustenance, lightning, and rain. Accordingly, heaven and earth stand by God’s command insofar as they remain in the natural condition suited to human existence. The divine call will come after this order has persisted; Resurrection is therefore concomitant with the destruction of the natural order. Likewise, the creation of heaven and earth is considered as connected with and beneficial to human life.

The passage surveys human existence from the species’ origin through sexual, linguistic, and color diversity, life within heaven and earth, livelihood, and sleep, to the natural order’s persistence for a fixed term before Resurrection. These matters bring the human species to completion and culminate in Resurrection. The distinct concluding calls to reflect, know, listen, and apply reason show an order: reflection yields knowledge, and hearing truths then yields understanding and comprehension. God knows best.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan says that, after establishing God’s lordship and divinity and reaching the question of Resurrection and return to Him, the passage supplies a logical proof of Resurrection’s possibility based on God’s creation and governance of the cosmos. To Him belongs all who are in the heavens and earth means that His dominion encompasses them all and that they will return to Him. Their existence depends on Him in every respect; nothing endures independently of Him. This is real dominion (mulk ḥaqīqī), and the sovereign (mālik) may dispose of His domain as He wills, including moving His servants from this world to the Hereafter.

Citing al-Rāghib, the commentary defines submissiveness (qunūt) as humble obedience. Here it is cosmic, rather than moral, obedience, since moral obedience can be contravened. It includes angels, jinn, and humans. Angels submit by their nature; humans and jinn remain subject to the cosmic order, even when they prevent one cause from operating through another cause within that same order. Their knowledge, desire, and free will all belong to it, so only what God wills—what has acquired its causes in objective reality—comes to pass. Nothing they will or desire occurs without His leave; He is therefore the true sovereign and master of them and all they possess.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains that to originate creation is to produce it without a prior likeness, while to bring it back is to produce it again after its first production. The verse calls restoration “more simple for Him,” which raises the objection that nothing can be harder or easier for infinite power.

Several proposed answers are rejected. Making “for Him” refer instead to creatures opposes the verse’s apparent wording. Taking ahwan to mean merely “very simple,” rather than comparative, is arbitrary. Comparing restoration and origination as acts in themselves fails because the verse expressly says “for Him.” Treating the comparison as only an accommodation to ordinary human standards has no textual indication. Al-Zamakhsharī’s further explanation—that restoration is obligatory for recompense while origination is voluntary, and hence nearer to realization—is also rejected: it rests on a false premise about priority and obligation; nearness to realization is a mental abstraction whereas ease and difficulty are real qualities relative to an agent; both origination and restoration are purposive and equally removed from impossibility; and the explanation ultimately reduces to the already rejected comparison between the acts themselves.

The commentary instead takes the following words as the rationale: “His is the loftiest description in the heavens and the earth.” Every perfection found in creatures—life, power, knowledge, sovereignty, generosity, greatness, and the like—is bestowed by God, limited, and accompanied by its contrary: creaturely knowledge is mixed with ignorance, life with essential death, and power with essential impotence. God possesses every such perfection in its absolute, pure, and unlimited form. Thus, if restoration is regarded among creatures as easier than first production, then for God it is pure ease, without any difficulty. This does not make origination difficult for Him, since difficulty decreases with an agent’s power and infinite power admits no difficulty in any act.

“And He is the All-mighty, the All-wise” explains this loftiest description. He is unconstrained because He has every perfection lacking in others, and His acts are flawless. Were any of His attributes limited or deficient relative to those of contingent beings, He would not be All-mighty, and His acts would consequently not be those of the All-wise.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan says that the verse gives a rhetorical, denial-invoking example drawn from people’s own circumstances. It asks whether masters would make their slaves partners in the wealth God has provided them, so that masters and slaves were equal in it and the masters feared using it without the slaves’ permission just as free people fear using jointly owned property without one another’s consent. The wording includes both masters and slaves, while the partnership necessarily entails equality in the property.

No master would make a slave a partner in his wealth, even though the master owns both the slave and the slave’s possessions. The parable therefore refutes the claim that angels, jinn, or other creatures who are God’s servants share His divinity and lordship. The closing statement that the signs are elaborated for people who apply reason prepares for what follows.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains that “Rather” turns from the preceding rational proof to the fact that the polytheists possess no rational basis for their belief: they follow desire without knowledge. They are called wrongdoers, rather than merely polytheists, because their wrongdoing explains why God leads them astray. Thus the question, “So who will guide those whom Allah has led astray?” denies that there is any hope of guidance for them despite the truth’s obviousness.

“They will have no helpers” means that their group will find none to rescue it from error and its consequences after God has led it astray. This plural wording does not mean that no individual among them can ever have a helper; others may receive help, such as intercession. The suggestion that the phrase necessarily means each person has no single helper is not required by ordinary usage. The verse therefore means that those who associate partners with God follow desire rather than knowledge or reason, are led astray because of their wrongdoing, and consequently have neither a guide nor helpers.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan takes the command to set one’s face toward the religion as the consequence of God’s exclusive creation and governance, His resurrection and judgment of mankind, and the absence of salvation for one who turns from Him. It may also console the Prophet: since polytheists follow desire through wrongdoing and are denied guidance and help, he and his faithful followers should concern themselves with the religion instead. To set one’s face means to attend to the religion without turning aside; the definite “the religion” apparently means Islam. Ḥanīfan most aptly qualifies the person addressed and means uprightness.

“Fiṭra” is the manner in which a thing is originated. The commentary takes “the origination of Allah” as an accusative of instigation: hold fast to the God-given human nature according to which mankind was created. Religion is a way of life leading to human happiness. As every creature is created with a nature, capacities, and guidance suited to reaching its perfection, human beings are created with a fiṭra that directs them to meet their deficiencies and needs and to recognize benefit and harm.

Human beings share one stable species, constituted of spirit and body; hence their happiness and misery as human beings, the general principles governing their action, and the guide leading to them must also be one. This guide is fiṭra, and “There is no altering Allah’s creation” indicates its unchanging character. If human happiness differed essentially between individuals, regions, or eras, a single society securing its members’ happiness could not exist, humanity would become many species, and social progress from deficiency to perfection would lack a common frame of reference. Differences of persons, places, and times do affect particular ways of life, but not the stable human reality on which the one upright religion rests.

The commentary rejects several alternatives. “Set your face” cannot simply mean acting rightly, since the face of an act is its goal, not the act itself. Reading fiṭra as “creed” (milla), whether explanatory or as a substitute for ḥanīf, conflicts with the apparent meaning of faṭara al-nās as creation and does not fit “There is no altering Allah’s creation”; nor can religion be reduced to Divine Unity while retaining these readings. Treating fiṭra as an absolute object for an implicit verb is plainly invalid. A reading that takes fiṭra as pointing specifically to a single eternal Creator is close to the preferred view, but improperly restricts a general verse to Divine Unity. Reading the negation in “There is no altering Allah’s creation” as a prohibition, including the view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās that it forbids castration, has no evidence for making creation mean religion or for calling denial of creation’s implications an alteration.

Fakhr al-Rāzī’s interpretation—according to which the phrase establishes unchangeable universal servanthood to God and refutes claims of release from moral duty, the idolaters’ hierarchy of stars, and the Christians’ claim about Jesus—is said to confuse cosmic and moral sovereignty and servanthood. Cosmic servanthood and worship are inseparable from created beings’ dependence on God and cannot change; religious, moral worship and servanthood can be altered or removed. If the verse concerns unalterable sovereignty, worship, and servanthood, it concerns their cosmic form, whereas Rāzī’s arguments concern their moral form.

The plural pronouns in the next verse shift the address from the Prophet to the community: set your faces toward the religion, turning to God in penitence. Being wary of Him includes obeying His commands and avoiding His prohibitions; prayer is singled out as a pillar of religion, and polytheism as among the gravest sins. “Of those who split up their religion” expounds the polytheists: they divide into sects, each pleased with what it possesses. Since they establish religion on fluctuating low desires rather than intellect, their religion cannot guide them. The prohibition of religious division is therefore, in reality, a prohibition against founding religion on desire rather than intellect. Treating this verse as detached from the preceding command does not fit the context.

Reading the negation in “There is no altering Allah’s creation” as a prohibition, including the view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās that it forbids castration, has no evidence for making creation mean religion or for calling denial of creation’s implications an alteration.

Fakhr al-Rāzī’s interpretation—according to which the phrase establishes unchangeable universal servanthood to God and refutes claims of release from moral duty, the idolaters’ hierarchy of stars, and the Christians’ claim about Jesus—is said to confuse cosmic and moral sovereignty and servanthood. Cosmic servanthood and worship are inseparable from created beings’ dependence on God and cannot change; religious, moral worship and servanthood can be altered or removed. If the verse concerns unalterable sovereignty, worship, and servanthood, it concerns their cosmic form, whereas Rāzī’s arguments concern their moral form.

The plural pronouns in the next verse shift the address from the Prophet to the community: set your faces toward the religion, turning to God in penitence. Being wary of Him includes obeying His commands and avoiding His prohibitions; prayer is singled out as a pillar of religion, and polytheism as among the gravest sins. “Of those who split up their religion” expounds the polytheists: they divide into sects, each pleased with what it possesses. Since they establish religion on fluctuating low desires rather than intellect, their religion cannot guide them. The prohibition of religious division is therefore, in reality, a prohibition against founding religion on desire rather than intellect. Treating this verse as detached from the preceding command does not fit the context.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan takes the command to set one’s face toward the religion as the consequence of God’s exclusive creation and governance, His resurrection and judgment of mankind, and the absence of salvation for one who turns from Him. It may also console the Prophet: since polytheists follow desire through wrongdoing and are denied guidance and help, he and his faithful followers should concern themselves with the religion instead. To set one’s face means to attend to the religion without turning aside; the definite “the religion” apparently means Islam. Ḥanīfan most aptly qualifies the person addressed and means uprightness.

“Fiṭra” is the manner in which a thing is originated. The commentary takes “the origination of Allah” as an accusative of instigation: hold fast to the God-given human nature according to which mankind was created. Religion is a way of life leading to human happiness. As every creature is created with a nature, capacities, and guidance suited to reaching its perfection, human beings are created with a fiṭra that directs them to meet their deficiencies and needs and to recognize benefit and harm.

Human beings share one stable species, constituted of spirit and body; hence their happiness and misery as human beings, the general principles governing their action, and the guide leading to them must also be one. This guide is fiṭra, and “There is no altering Allah’s creation” indicates its unchanging character. If human happiness differed essentially between individuals, regions, or eras, a single society securing its members’ happiness could not exist, humanity would become many species, and social progress from deficiency to perfection would lack a common frame of reference. Differences of persons, places, and times do affect particular ways of life, but not the stable human reality on which the one upright religion rests.

The commentary rejects several alternatives. “Set your face” cannot simply mean acting rightly, since the face of an act is its goal, not the act itself. Reading fiṭra as “creed” (milla), whether explanatory or as a substitute for ḥanīf, conflicts with the apparent meaning of faṭara al-nās as creation and does not fit “There is no altering Allah’s creation”; nor can religion be reduced to Divine Unity while retaining these readings. verses.33: Al-Mizan notes that “touches” (mass), as well as the indefiniteness of distress and mercy, indicates even a slight affliction. When illness, hardship, poverty, or another small distress reaches people, they call upon their Lord and turn penitently to Him. Yet when He lets them taste mercy, a portion of those who had acknowledged His lordship associate partners with Him again, showing ingratitude through their actions. The wording “a part of them” indicates that not all behave in this way.
verses.34: Al-Mizan explains that this is a warning to the polytheists who become ungrateful after God lets them taste mercy. The lām in li yakfurū introduces an imperative, and “So enjoy!” is another imperative; both are threats. The shift from a third-person command to a second-person command conveys God’s anger at their negligence: they call on Him in hardship but are ungrateful in ease.
verses.35: Al-Mizan takes “Or” as truncated (munqatiʿ), beginning a new question: has God informed them of an authority, meaning evidence, that proves the partners they associate with Him? On this reading, “sending down” means informing and “speak” means proving. Alternatively, “authority” may mean a sovereign possessing authority; then the question is whether God has sent down a sovereign who speaks of what they associate with Him, without figurative usage.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan explains that “taste,” like “touch” in the preceding verse, suggests even a small amount. The first idhā is conditional, whereas the second expresses astonishment. The contrast shows that divine mercy is abundant and certain, while ill is scarce and only possible. Mercy is attributed to God because it is a real reality (wujūdī) overflowing from Him; ill is privative (ʿadamī), the absence of such an overflow. Ill is accordingly connected to what people’s hands have sent ahead, whereas no cause is given for mercy, because it is pure grace (tafaḍḍul).

Their exultation in mercy and their sudden despondency at ill reveal superficiality: they rejoice at what they desire without recognizing its dependence on God’s will, and despair when deprived as though deprivation too were not under His will. Although both are in God’s hand, mercy is more abundant; the present tense for their despondency also presents it as transient.

There is no contradiction with the preceding statement that, when distress touches people, they supplicate their Lord penitently. Here they are described as rejoicing when they obtain what they want and, when they do not, despairing and calling upon God in that despondency. Suggestions that the two verses concern different groups or states, that supplication is outward while despair is inward, or that despair means hoarding wealth, are unwarranted and do not fit the verse’s astonishment at their despondency.
verses.37: Al-Mizan says that the verse exposes the error of quickly exulting over mercy or despairing over ill. The expansion and tightening of provision (rizq) depend wholly on God’s will, so what one possesses may be removed and what one suffers may be relieved. Provision may appear visible and secure, but obtaining it depends on countless factors, of which the person and whatever reassures him are only individual factors. All ultimately return to God, who gives and withholds, expands and contracts provision; this is a sign for those with faith.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan explains that dhū al-qurbā means a blood relative, miskīn one in a worse condition than a faqīr, and ibn al-sabīl a needy wayfarer. The phrase “his right” shows that the relative has an inalienable right.

Because the verse addresses the Prophet, its apparent contextual meaning, if it is Medinan, concerns khums: the relative is the Prophet’s relatives, and the duty first belongs to the Prophet and then to whoever is responsible for khums after him. If, however, it is Meccan like the other verses of the sūrah, it enjoins generosity generally toward relatives, the needy, and travellers. In either case, its stated benefit is general: those who seek Allah’s pleasure by this giving are the felicitous.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan explains that ribāʾ literally denotes the growth of wealth, and li yarbū indicates why it bears this name. Wealth given to others in order to increase their wealth, rather than seeking God’s pleasure, does not increase with Allah: it earns no divine reward. Zakāt here means charity in the broad sense—giving wealth for God’s sake without squandering it—and those who give it seeking Allah’s pleasure receive a manifold, that is doubled, increase in their wealth or reward.

If the verse is Meccan, the contextual contrast is between permitted ribāʾ, a gift given without intending God’s pleasure, and charity given for His sake. If it is Medinan, ribāʾ means prohibited usury and zakāt the obligatory zakāt. The commentary judges this verse and the preceding one more similar to Medinan than Meccan verses, and finds no valid basis in narrations or consensus for claims concerning their provenance.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan explains that the rhetorical question denies that any alleged partner can create, provide, cause death, or give life. Since these are attributes of divinity and lordship, and none of the invented deities performs them, God alone is the deity and lord.

Provision (rizq) is inseparable from creation: it is a relation among created things in which some sustain the existence of others, and is therefore itself a kind of creation. Hence the idolaters cannot concede creation to God while assigning provision, life, death, human affairs, good, or evil to other gods. All such functions belong to the Creator, leaving no dominion for the alleged partners; thus God is immaculate and exalted above their association.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan takes the verse generally, not as confined to a particular place, time, or event: land and sea mean the whole earthly surface. Corruption (fasād) includes every hardship that disrupts the proper natural order and human life—such as earthquakes, drought, famine, epidemics, war, raids, and insecurity—whether or not its immediate occurrence is ascribed to human choice.

It appears because of people's deeds, especially association with God and sin. Human virtue and corruption directly correspond to, and affect, cosmic events. The purposive phrase li yudhīqahum means that God makes people taste the evil consequences in which their own deeds themselves appear. They taste the recompense of some of what they have done, not merely some of its recompense, because in mercy God forgives much; this concerns worldly consequences, not deferred punishment in the Hereafter. Its purpose is that they return from idolatry and sin to divine unity and obedience.

The verse thus follows the preceding proof of divine unity by showing the corruption resulting from shirk, a grave maʿṣiya. Al-Mizan rejects restricted readings of land and sea—whether as Mecca, particular deserts and river or coastal settlements, nomadic and settled regions, barren and fertile areas, or land and the cities of the sea—as forced attempts to fit reports about Mecca's drought following the Prophet's supplication against Quraysh. It also regards as plainly weak the interpretation that land refers to Adam's son killing his brother and sea to the king's seizure of ships in the story of Khiḍr.
verses.42: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is commanded to tell people to travel and behold the ruins of earlier peoples: their houses lie in rubble, their traces have vanished, and their people were destroyed by calamities. Since most of them associated partners with God, He made them taste some consequences of their deeds so that they might take warning and return to divine unity. Their fate externally confirms the preceding verse.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan presents the verse as the conclusion from the consequences of associating partners with God and rejecting truth: one must set one's heart on the upright religion before the Day of Resurrection, a day from God that nothing can repel.

On that Day people will be split. This may mean either division between paradise and hell or separation in which each person stands alone, as in The day mankind will be like scattered moths (101:4). Both are possible, but the division between paradise and hell is apparently closer to the meaning.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan takes (30:44) as explaining the division on the Day of Resurrection. The faithless are one group: they meet either the consequences of their faithlessness or their faithlessness itself, transformed into an everlasting blaze. The righteous are the other group. Their righteous deeds, which prosper only with faith, prepare for them the means of life and subsistence in the Hereafter, as one spreads out a mattress.

The purpose in (30:45) is that God reward those who have faith and do righteous deeds out of His grace. Jazāʾ conveys both sufficing and reciprocal requital: good for good and evil for evil. Yet there is no conflict between recompense and grace, for people and their deeds wholly belong to God; as slaves, they possess nothing independently by which to deserve a reward. Whatever He gives is therefore unearned faḍl.

Nevertheless, through grace and mercy, God treats them as owners of their deeds and grants them a due in return, making paradise and nearness to Him a recompense for those deeds. Even this assigned due remains grace. It arises from His love for those who love their Lord, set their hearts on the upright religion, and follow His Messenger: Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins, and Allah is all-forgiving, all-merciful (3:31). Thus the reward is both reciprocal recompense and grace flowing from divine love, whereas He does not love the faithless.

verses.46:
Al-Mizan explains that winds are bearers of good news because they precede rain. God sends them both to announce this good and to let people taste His mercy through the many benefits they bring, including such things as pollinating trees and cleansing the air.

Ships sail by His command through wind currents, and people seek His grace—that is, His sustenance (rizq)). These are visible purposes of the winds. Their spiritual purpose is that people give thanks (shukr): use blessings in a manner that indicates their Source, praise that Source for His blessing, and ultimately worship Him. The use of laʿalla rather than the purposive lām indicates a wish that this gratitude occur, since such a spiritual purpose may remain unfulfilled.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan notes, following al-Rāghib, that ajrama is metaphorically used for doing something blameworthy or unpleasant, rather than for a praiseworthy act.

The verse is an aside explaining that God has assigned the faithful a right over Himself: He will help them in this world and the next, and take vengeance on those who were guilty. This does not mean that anyone compels or commands God. The implicative fāʾ in Then We took vengeance implies that, after the apostles brought manifest proofs, some believed while others became guilty; God then took vengeance on the guilty. His help to the faithful consists in saving them from punishment and destroying their enemies, so that this vengeance was undertaken on their behalf and was itself a form of help (naṣr).
verses.48:
Al-Mizan explains that God sends the winds to move and spread the saḥāb in the samāʾ, arranging it into kisaf from which wadq issues through its khilāl. He sends this rain upon whichever servants He wills, and they rejoice because it sustains them, their crops, and their herds.

They had previously been in iblās, akin to yaʾs or qunūṭ. The rain is the referent of “it was sent down.” “Earlier” (min qablih) may reinforce their state immediately before the rain, showing the rapid change from despair to joy; as al-Kashshāf holds, it may instead emphasize that their prolonged waiting had made their despair intense, and thus their joy proportionate. It is also possible that the pronoun in min qablih refers to the sending of the winds: they remained despondent until the winds came.
verses.49:

verses.50:
Al-Mizan explains that Allah’s mercy is the rain sent from clouds spread by the winds, while its āthār, or results, are the earth’s renewed life—its plants, trees, and fruits. The entire system of winds, clouds, rain, and resulting vegetation manifests this mercy.

“Indeed That is the reviver of the dead” refers to God; the distant demonstrative magnifies and glorifies Him. Though the visible example is the dead earth, the intended dead are human beings and other living creatures. In both cases, death is the absence of the effects of life from something preserved, and revival is their return. Since this is visibly realized in the earth and its vegetation, the revival of human beings and other creatures is likewise possible. Moreover, God’s absolute power necessarily includes bringing the dead back to life; otherwise it would not be unlimited.
verses.51: Al-Mizan takes “it” in “they see it turn yellow” to mean the vegetation. The oath-consequent gives the sense that, if God sends a cold wind that yellows their crops and trees, they will surely become ungrateful for His blessings. The verse reproves people who shift with changing fortune: they quickly rejoice in blessings, but when God removes some of His grace, they immediately deny even evident blessings. Interpretations referring “it” to yellow clouds that will not rain, or to the wind because rīḥ may be masculine or feminine, are unlikely.
verses.52: Al-Mizan explains that God consoles His Messenger not to grieve over those who fluctuate between joy and despondency yet disbelieve because they neither believe in nor reflect upon the signs. They are like the dead, deaf, and blind, whom he cannot make hear or guide. Only those who reflect upon the arguments, believe in God’s signs, and submit can hear and be guided.
verses.53: Al-Mizan explains that God consoles His Messenger not to grieve over those who fluctuate between joy and despondency yet disbelieve because they neither believe in nor reflect upon the signs. They are like the dead, deaf, and blind, whom he cannot make hear or guide. Only those who reflect upon the arguments, believe in God’s signs, and submit can hear and be guided.
verses.54: Al-Mizan explains that “from weakness” (min al-ḍaʿf) marks the beginning of human creation: weakness (ḍaʿf), apparently infancy though it may also mean the seed, is followed by power (quwwa), meaning maturity, and then by weakness and old age. Old age (shayba) explicates the latter weakness. The indefinite forms of weakness and power indicate that their degrees are unspecified, since individuals differ. Each successive condition is willed and created by God, not by a deity particular to human beings as idol-worshipers claim; hence the closing description of Him as the All-knowing, the All-powerful.
verses.55: Al-Mizan presents this verse as an afterword to the preceding signs of God’s oneness and the Resurrection and as preparation for the Chapter’s conclusion. It exposes people who receive true speech as falsehood and clear signs as meaningless; their habitual turning from truth to falsehood leaves them without excuse. This disposition remains with them at the Resurrection: having been in their graves between death and resurrection, they will swear that only an hour has passed. Unable to distinguish the Day of Resurrection from the world, they take it for an ordinary worldly hour. Their statement is thus another instance of their former lying, when they called truth, proofs, and evidences falsehood or superstition.
verses.56:
Al-Mizan explains that those given knowledge and faith answer the guilty, who imagine that they remained only an hour because of their attachment to this world and their inability to perceive the difference between it and the Day of Resurrection. The faithful know that the interval between this world and that Day is described as: And ahead of them is a barrier until the day they will be resurrected (23:100). They therefore identify the present day as the Day of Resurrection, whereas the guilty, lacking certainty about what lies beyond this world, think only an hour has passed.

“Given knowledge and faith” means possessing certainty (yaqīn) concerning God and His signs and adhering to what that certainty requires regarding His gifts. “Allah’s Book” (kitāb allāh) apparently means the divine scriptures, or the Qur’an alone. Al-Mizan rejects the proposed unusual word order (taqdīm wa taʾkhīr) that would make the phrase mean that those given knowledge and faith in God’s Book will speak.
verses.57: Al-Mizan defines “propitiation” (ʿutbā) as acknowledging one’s wrongdoing in an effort to appease one’s rebuker. On that day, wrongdoers’ excuses will not benefit them, nor will they be required to undertake anything to avert rebuke. An author’s note adds that “God’s Book” may possibly refer to the Guarded Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), based on This is Our book, which speaks truly against you (45:29), according to the later explanation of that verse.
verses.58: Al-Mizan explains that, because their hearts have been sealed and they are far from truth, no parable can draw them toward it. If brought a sign, they will accuse its bearer of fabricating falsehood, for they see every truth as falsehood. The Qur’an’s use of “the faithless” (alladhīna kafarū), rather than a pronoun, indicates that their faithlessness is the reason for this response.
verses.59: Al-Mizan explains that God seals the hearts of those who do not know Him or His signs, including the Resurrection, while they wilfully persist in ignorance and doubt.
verses.60: Al-Mizan instructs the Prophet to endure their accusation, “You are nothing but fabricators!”, as well as their derision and scorn. God’s promise to help the faithful is true, so he must not be troubled by those who have no conviction in that promise. The alternative interpretation that their lack of conviction concerns the clear signs recited to them is baseless: the Chapter begins and ends with the promise of help for the faithful.
